Issued at 154 PM CDT Sat Aug 29 2026

Early this afternoon, a broad and strong mid/upper ridge was 
centered over the southern and central plains with a vigorous deep 
layer trough progressing eastward out of the PNW. Out ahead of this 
trough, several perturbations were noted within southwesterly upper 
flow over the northern CONUS. Despite the copious amounts of upper 
level cloud cover across the region, modest destabilization is 
occurring this afternoon across North Dakota out ahead of shallow 
shortwave trough located over the central Rockies. As forcing for 
ascent arrives later this evening into tonight, isolated to 
scattered showers and storms are expected to develop across western 
North Dakota and gradually work their way eastward. Continued 
development and/or persistence of this activity may also be 
supported by subtle mid-level WAA overnight into early Sunday 
morning. The greatest coverage of showers and storms will likely be 
along and south of I-94, especially given that better forcing for 
ascent appears to be trending further south for tonight into early 
tomorrow morning. Activity this evening into tonight will struggle 
to contend with widespread convective inhibition, and chances for a 
couple of isolated severe storms before 06Z appears to be waning 
given the latest short term guidance. However, elevated instability 
along the axis of mid-level WAA overnight into early Sunday morning 
will be fairly decent (generally around 1500-2000 J/kg of MUCAPE). 
Effective shear around 30 knots could support some organized 
elevated convection capable of hail up to ping pong ball size. 
Damaging wind gusts appears less likely, but an isolated instance of 
a 50-60 mph wind gust cannot be ruled out overnight and early Sunday 
morning.

Sunday appears to be quite the complicated setup for potential 
severe weather across North Dakota. A strong and deep upper trough 
will lumber eastward across southern Alberta during the day on 
Sunday with a sharp lobe of vorticity expected to round the southern 
end of the trough and kick out across eastern Montana and North 
Dakota. This should provide significant forcing for ascent across 
the northern CONUS for widespread showers and thunderstorms Sunday 
afternoon through Sunday night. Guidance has generally backed off 
the idea that shower and thunderstorm activity will be ongoing 
through much of the morning hours on Sunday. This seems a little off 
given the amplitude of upper level diffluence that will be 
overspreading the region as early as Sunday morning, but it's likely 
other factors are at play such as subsidence behind any activity the 
occurs late tonight into early Sunday morning. With short-range 
models backing off on morning convection across the state, this 
leaves the door open for potent destabilization across the forecast 
area. Model soundings across the warm sector Sunday afternoon show 
an uncapped airmass with ample instability around 2000-2500 J/kg. 
Shear will also be conducive for some organized convection with 0-6 
km shear around 25 to 35 knots. Given the amount of synoptic ascent, 
the sharpness of the surface frontal boundary, and shear vectors 
parallel to said boundary, the expectation is for thunderstorms to 
rapidly grow upscale. With a linear storm mode favored, the main 
concern will be damaging wind gusts around 60-70 mph. At this time, 
it appears the hail threat will be limited to the first couple of 
hours after convective initiation when storms still have the 
opportunity to be semi-discrete. Lastly, a tornado or two cannot be 
ruled out where surface winds will be slightly back along a weak 
warm front draped across the state. The primary difference in the 
guidance at this point is the location of the warm sector. 
Solutions, like the HRRR and ARW, show a psuedo-dryline developing 
in the vicinity of the US-83 keeping warm, humid air east of this 
corridor. Meanwhile, other solutions, like the NAM and NSSL, show 
this moisture gradient along the ND/MT state line. This may have an 
impact on the intensity of convection early, perhaps modestly 
suppressing thunderstorm activity in the drier solution. However, 
the overall severe threats remain the same regardless of which 
scenario plays out.

Monday also appears to be a somewhat busy day for much of North 
Dakota, though more for wind and fire weather concerns. The surface 
low and upper low are forecast to become more vertically stacked 
over Saskatchewan, and a tight pressure gradient is expected across 
southern Saskatchewan/Manitoba into much of North Dakota. Mostly 
clear skies should allow for deep mixing across these areas, and 
uniform flow in the boundary layer should allow for efficient mixing 
of stout winds to the surface. Model guidance suggests 850 mb winds 
could be in the neighborhood of 45 to 50 knots, mainly across
